sections.description: This section introduces the patient’s presenting complaints, vital findings, and key physical exam features that prompt a high‑yield differential. It also outlines the early laboratory and imaging work‑up that set the stage for recognizing an unusual combination of infectious, inflammatory, and endocrine disorders.
subtopics: Chief complaints: fever, headache, oral aphthae, fatigue, hiccups, arthralgia
Vital signs and basic physical exam findings
Initial laboratory abnormalities: hyponatraemia, hyperglycaemia, elevated CK and liver enzymes, CRP, ESR
Early imaging: unremarkable chest X‑ray, CT of head, chest and abdomen
Differential at the bedside: CNS infection vs systemic inflammatory disease vs endocrine disturbance

sections.section_title: 2. Diagnostic Reasoning for Behçet’s Disease and Neuro‑Behçet’s Disease
sections.description: This section explains how clinicians moved from the non‑specific systemic picture to a definitive diagnosis of Behçet’s disease, incorporating the International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease (ICBD). It then addresses the criteria for acute neuro‑Behçet’s disease and the importance of CSF findings and normal MRI in this context.
subtopics: ICBD scoring: oral ulcers, genital ulcers, folliculitis‑like rash, HLA‑B51, fever and fatigue
Timing of neurological involvement: simultaneous vs delayed onset
CSF profile in acute neuro‑BD: mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, normal opening pressure
Normal brain MRI in early neuro‑BD: clinical implications
Role of additional tests (ACE, sIL‑2R, viral PCRs) in ruling out mimickers

sections.section_title: 3. Identification and Management of SIADH in the Context of CNS Inflammation
sections.description: This section focuses on the endocrine component—syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion—to show how hyponatraemia was recognised, classified, and safely managed. It also discusses the pathophysiological link between CNS inflammation, cytokines, and ADH release.
subtopics: Diagnostic criteria for SIADH: euvolemia, low serum osmolality, high urine osmolality and sodium, elevated ADH
Potential drivers of SIADH in CNS disease: IL‑6, cerebral inflammation, hypothalamic involvement
Clinical presentation clues: persistent hiccups, rhabdomyolysis
Fluid restriction protocol and monitoring of serum sodium
When to consider hypertonic saline or vasopressin antagonists

sections.section_title: 4. Therapeutic Strategy: Colchicine Monotherapy in Acute Neuro‑Behçet’s Disease
sections.description: This section evaluates the treatment approach, detailing why colchicine was chosen, its mechanisms of action, evidence for efficacy in mucocutaneous and neuro‑Behçet’s disease, and comparison with standard corticosteroid or immunosuppressive regimens.
subtopics: Rationale for colchicine: inhibition of neutrophil migration, IL‑1β and IL‑6 suppression
Evidence base: systematic reviews, case series, and guidelines
Toxicity profile and monitoring requirements
Response assessment: resolution of fever, mucocutaneous lesions, normalisation of sodium, CK, and CRP
Long‑term management: continuation for 4 years, transition to glycaemic control therapy

sections.description: This final section synthesises the case into actionable learning points, emphasising diagnostic vigilance for neuro‑Behçet’s disease in patients with mucocutaneous features and hyponatraemia, the importance of a judicious work‑up, and the potential role of colchicine as an alternative to steroids.
subtopics: High index of suspicion for neuro‑BD in febrile, hyponatraemic patients with oral/genital ulcers
When a normal MRI does not exclude neuro‑BD
SIADH as a marker of CNS inflammation
Colchicine as a steroid‑sparing option in selected neuro‑BD cases
Key warning signs of severe hyponatraemia: hiccups, rhabdomyolysis
